blocks.text: Tissue culture in agriculture

Biotechnology is the use of living organisms, or their parts, to make products and services useful to humans. In agriculture its aims are to raise yield, to protect crops and to reduce the use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides. One of the oldest tools is **plant tissue culture**.

The technique of growing cells, tissues or organs of a plant in a sterile, nutrient-rich artificial medium under controlled conditions. A small piece of plant used to start the culture is called an explant.

Tissue culture works because of **totipotency**, the ability of a living plant cell to give rise to a complete plant when it is given the right conditions. The explant is placed on a sterile medium containing sucrose as the carbon source, mineral salts, vitamins, amino acids and the plant growth regulators **auxin** and **cytokinin**. The cells divide into an unorganised mass, the callus, which is then induced to form shoots and roots by changing the ratio of the hormones. The small plantlets are later transferred to soil after hardening. By this method thousands of genetically identical plants (clones, also called somaclones) can be obtained quickly from one parent plant, and the method is called **micropropagation**. Many important food plants such as tomato, banana and apple are propagated this way on a commercial scale.

Tissue culture also helps to recover **healthy, disease-free plants**. Even if the plant is infected with a virus, the meristem, the growing tip at the apex or in the axil of a leaf, is usually free of the virus. When a meristem is removed and grown in vitro, the virus-free plants that develop can be multiplied. Another use is **somatic hybridisation**: the cell walls of two different plants are removed by enzymes to give protoplasts, which are fused to form a hybrid. The hybrid between tomato and potato, called the **pomato**, was produced this way, although it did not have all the desired characters.

Tissue culture rests on totipotency. Auxin plus cytokinin control callus, shoot and root formation. Meristem culture gives virus-free plants. Protoplast fusion gives somatic hybrids such as the pomato. Micropropagation gives large numbers of identical plants.
Genetically modified organisms and their uses

Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are called **genetically modified organisms (GMOs)**. A GM plant is a plant that carries a foreign gene, called a transgene, which gives it a useful new property. GM plants have been useful in many ways. They have been made **tolerant to abiotic stresses** such as cold, drought, salt and heat. They are **pest-resistant**, which decreases the use of chemical pesticides. They **reduce post-harvest losses**. They show **increased efficiency of mineral usage by plants**, which prevents early exhaustion of fertility of the soil. They have **enhanced nutritional value of food**: for example, Golden Rice is a variety that is rich in vitamin A, because it makes beta-carotene. GM crops are also used to produce **tailor-made plants** that supply alternative resources to industries such as starches, fuels and pharmaceuticals.
An organism whose genetic material has been changed by recombinant DNA technology, by adding, removing or altering a gene, so that it shows a new trait that does not occur naturally in that organism.
Bt cotton

Bt cotton is the best-known GM crop in India. The name comes from the soil bacterium *Bacillus thuringiensis*. It forms protein crystals during a particular phase of its growth. These crystals contain a toxic insecticidal protein, the **Cry protein**. The Bt toxin does not kill the bacterium because it exists there as an inactive **protoxin**. Once an insect ingests the crystals, the alkaline pH of the insect gut dissolves them and activates the toxin. The activated toxin binds to the surface of the midgut epithelial cells and creates pores. The cells swell and burst (lyse), and the insect dies.

The genes that code for these proteins are called *cry* genes. Specific *cry* genes act against particular groups of insects: the proteins encoded by *cryIAc* and *cryIIAb* control the cotton bollworms, while *cryIAb* controls the corn borer. The relevant gene was isolated from *Bacillus thuringiensis* and incorporated into the cotton plant. The plant then makes the toxin in its own tissues and a bollworm that feeds on it dies. This reduces the need to spray chemical insecticides on the crop.

Exam tip: the insect gut is alkaline, and that is the reason a protoxin is activated only in insects. A common wrong answer is that the toxin is active inside the bacterium; it is not, which is why the bacterium is safe from its own poison.
RNA interference

**RNA interference (RNAi)** is a cellular defence in eukaryotes in which a gene is silenced by a complementary double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). The dsRNA binds to the messenger RNA (mRNA) of the gene and prevents its translation, so the protein is not made. This is silencing of the specific mRNA.

RNAi has been used to protect tobacco plants from a nematode, *Meloidogyne incognita*, which infects tobacco roots and greatly reduces the yield. A strategy was adopted to prevent this infection, based on RNAi. Using *Agrobacterium* as a vector, nematode-specific genes were introduced into the host plant. The introduction of DNA was such that it produced both sense and antisense RNA in the host cell. These two RNAs, being complementary to each other, formed a double-stranded RNA that initiated RNAi and thus silenced the specific mRNA of the nematode. The consequence was that the parasite could not survive in a transgenic host that expresses the specific interfering RNA. The transgenic plant was therefore protected from the parasite.

blocks.problem: A student wants to explain why a transgenic tobacco plant that produces both sense and antisense RNA of a nematode gene resists the parasite. Write the explanation in steps.
blocks.solution: Step 1: the sense and antisense RNAs made in the plant cell are complementary, so they pair to form double-stranded RNA. Step 2: the double-stranded RNA starts RNA interference, which is a silencing mechanism. Step 3: when the nematode feeds on the root, the specific RNA enters the parasite and binds to the complementary mRNA of the nematode gene. Step 4: that mRNA cannot be translated, so the essential protein is not made and the nematode cannot survive.
blocks.answer: Double-stranded RNA silences the nematode mRNA, so the parasite dies and the plant is protected.

blocks.text: Biotechnology in medicine: genetically engineered insulin

Biotechnology has transformed the production of medicines. Recombinant DNA technology makes therapeutic proteins in large quantity and with no risk of an immune reaction. The classic example is **insulin**, the hormone used by people with diabetes mellitus to control blood sugar. Earlier, insulin was extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs. This often caused an allergic or other immune reaction in some patients because the animal insulin is not identical to the human hormone.

Insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains: chain **A** of 21 amino acids and chain **B** of 30 amino acids, linked together by disulphide bridges. In humans, it is synthesised as a pro-hormone, **proinsulin**, which also contains an extra stretch called the **C peptide**. The C peptide is removed during maturation to give mature insulin. The main problem in making insulin by recombinant DNA was assembling the mature form. In 1983, the company Eli Lilly prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains of human insulin and introduced them into plasmids of *E. coli* to produce the chains separately. The A and B chains produced were extracted and combined by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin. The product is sold as **Humulin**.

blocks.problem: How many amino acids are present in the mature human insulin made from the separately produced A and B chains, and why is there no C peptide in the product?
blocks.solution: Chain A has 21 amino acids and chain B has 30 amino acids, so the mature molecule has 21 + 30 = 51 amino acids. The two chains are joined by disulphide bridges. In the natural body, proinsulin contains an additional C peptide that is removed during maturation. In the recombinant method, the A and B chains are made separately from their own DNA sequences, so the C peptide is never present and the chains are simply joined.
blocks.answer: 51 amino acids; the C peptide is absent because A and B are made separately.

blocks.text: Gene therapy

**Gene therapy** is a collection of methods that allow the correction of a gene defect diagnosed in a child or embryo. Genes are inserted into a person's cells and tissues to treat a hereditary disease. Correction of a genetic defect involves delivery of a normal gene into the individual or embryo to take over the function of, and compensate for, the non-functional gene.

The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a four-year-old girl with **adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency**. The enzyme is crucial for the functioning of the immune system. The disorder is caused by the deletion of the gene for ADA. In some children it can be cured by bone marrow transplantation, and in others by enzyme replacement therapy, in which functional ADA is given by injection. The problem is that the patient requires periodic infusion. In gene therapy, lymphocytes from the blood of the patient are grown in a culture outside the body. A functional ADA cDNA, using a retroviral vector, is then introduced into these lymphocytes, which are subsequently returned to the patient. However, as these cells are not immortal, the patient requires periodic infusion of such genetically engineered lymphocytes. If the gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages, it could be a permanent cure.
Molecular diagnosis

Early detection of a disease helps in effective treatment. With conventional methods of diagnosis (serum and urine analysis and so on) early detection is not possible, because a disease is noticed only when symptoms appear. Three molecular tools help diagnose at a very early stage.

blocks.caption: Tools of molecular diagnosis
rows: Amplification of nucleic acid so that even very small amounts become detectable
Detecting HIV in suspected AIDS patients; detecting gene mutations in suspected cancer patients
A single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule (probe) hybridises with its complementary DNA; the signal appears on a photographic film
Finding a clone that carries a mutated gene; the mutated gene does not hybridise with the probe, so the clone does not appear on the film
Antigen-antibody interaction: infection is detected by antigens (proteins, glycoproteins) or by antibodies synthesised against the pathogen
Detecting a pathogen in the body, such as HIV

blocks.problem: A virus is present in the blood of a patient in only a few copies. A laboratory uses PCR to amplify a segment of the viral DNA. If each cycle doubles the number of copies, how many copies will be made from one starting copy after 30 cycles, and why is PCR useful for early diagnosis?
blocks.solution: Each cycle doubles the number of copies, so after n cycles the number of copies is 2 raised to n. For n = 30 this is 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 copies, which is about one billion. A single copy that cannot be detected can therefore be amplified to a quantity that is easily detected, even before the disease causes symptoms.
blocks.answer: 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 copies; PCR makes a very small amount of pathogen DNA detectable early.

blocks.text: Transgenic animals
An animal whose DNA has been manipulated so that it possesses and expresses an extra (foreign) gene. More than 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.

Transgenic animals are made to help in several areas. **Normal physiology and development**: studying how genes regulate the body, for example the effect of insulin-like growth factor. **Study of disease**: models for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's disease have been created to learn how genes contribute to disease and to design new therapies. **Biological products**: a transgenic animal can make useful products. For example, human protein alpha-1-antitrypsin is used to treat emphysema, and similar work is being done for phenylketonuria (PKU) and cystic fibrosis. In 1997 the first transgenic cow, **Rosie**, produced human alpha-lactalbumin-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre). The milk was a nutritionally more balanced product for human babies than natural cow milk. **Vaccine safety**: transgenic mice are used to test the safety of a vaccine before it is used on humans, for example the polio vaccine. **Chemical safety testing (toxicity testing)**: transgenic animals are made more sensitive to toxic substances than non-transgenic animals, so the effects appear faster and with fewer animals.

blocks.problem: Rosie's milk contained 2.4 grams of human alpha-lactalbumin per litre. How much of the protein would 5 litres contain, and is the protein a natural component of cow milk?
blocks.solution: The amount of protein is concentration multiplied by volume: 2.4 grams per litre x 5 litres = 12 grams. Human alpha-lactalbumin is a human protein; the cow has no gene for it. Rosie produced it only because the human gene had been introduced into her, which is why she is called a transgenic animal and why the milk was nutritionally more balanced for babies.
blocks.answer: 12 g; no, it is a foreign human protein expressed through the introduced transgene.

blocks.text: Ethical issues: biopiracy and patents

Manipulating living organisms raises ethical and safety questions. Is it right to put a human gene in a cow, or to change the genetic makeup of an organism? The effect of GM organisms on the environment, other species and human health is not fully known. In India the **Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC)** takes decisions on the validity of GM research and on the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services.
The use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and the people concerned, and without compensatory payment to them.
A right granted by a government to an inventor to prevent others from commercial use of the invention for a limited period, usually 20 years. It encourages the inventor to disclose the invention.

Many industrialised nations are rich in financial resources but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge, while developing nations are rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge. This imbalance has led to biopiracy. A well-known case is the patent granted in 1997 by the US Patent Office to an American company on a variety of **basmati rice**, whose characteristics were already known in India. India has thousands of varieties of rice, and basmati is one of them, so the patent was seen as taking over a traditional resource. Such claims have to be opposed legally, and to guard against them India has laws such as the Biodiversity Act and amendments of its Patents Act.

GM crops help yield and nutrition but need safety checks (GEAC in India). Biopiracy is unauthorised, uncompensated use of bio-resources or traditional knowledge. Patents give the inventor exclusive rights for a limited period (20 years).

Common mistake: confusing RNAi with antisense therapy of the whole genome, or saying Bt toxin is active inside Bacillus. Another trap: gene therapy by lymphocytes is not permanent; only correction at the early embryonic stage could be permanent.

questions.stem: The ability of a single plant cell to grow into a complete plant under suitable conditions is called
questions.explanation: Totipotency is the capacity of a plant cell to give rise to a whole plant, and it is the basis of tissue culture. Micropropagation is the use of this ability to make many plants, and dedifferentiation is the return of a mature cell to a dividing callus.

optionRationale.2: Dedifferentiation is the return of mature cells to a dividing mass, not the ability to form a whole plant.
optionRationale.3: Hybridisation is the cross between different varieties or fused cells.
optionRationale.4: Micropropagation is the technique that uses totipotency, not the ability itself.

questions.stem: The Bt toxin is not toxic to Bacillus thuringiensis itself because the toxin in the bacterium is
options: stored in the cell wall as a lipid
questions.explanation: Bacillus thuringiensis stores the Cry protein as crystals of an inactive protoxin. It is activated only when an insect swallows the crystals and the alkaline gut pH dissolves them. So the bacterium is protected from its own toxin.

optionRationale.1: The toxin is present in the bacterium, in the form of crystals.
optionRationale.3: There is no antitoxin gene involved; the protein is simply inactive.
optionRationale.4: The toxin is a protein, not a lipid.

questions.objective: Explain why Bt is safe for the bacterium

questions.stem: Which of the following was the first transgenic cow, which produced human alpha-lactalbumin enriched milk?
questions.explanation: Rosie, produced in 1997, was the first transgenic cow and her milk contained human alpha-lactalbumin at 2.4 grams per litre. Dolly was a cloned sheep, Humulin is human insulin and Golden Rice is a vitamin A-rich rice variety.

optionRationale.1: Dolly was a cloned sheep and not a transgenic cow.
optionRationale.2: Humulin is the trade name of recombinant human insulin.
optionRationale.4: Golden refers to Golden Rice, not to an animal.

questions.stem: In the rDNA production of human insulin by Eli Lilly, the A and B chains were produced separately in
questions.explanation: In 1983 Eli Lilly prepared DNA sequences for chain A and chain B of human insulin and introduced them into plasmids of Escherichia coli. The two chains were then extracted and joined by disulphide bonds to form human insulin.

optionRationale.1: Agrobacterium is used for transferring genes into plants.
optionRationale.2: Yeast was not the host of the original Eli Lilly method.
optionRationale.3: Bacillus thuringiensis supplies the cry genes for Bt crops, not insulin.

questions.objective: Name the host used for rDNA insulin

questions.stem: A farmer has a banana plant infected with a virus and wants virus-free plants for multiplication. The best tissue-culture approach is to culture the
questions.explanation: The apical or axillary meristem is usually free from virus even in an infected plant. When it is excised and grown in vitro, virus-free plantlets develop and can be multiplied. Mature leaf, root hair and woody tissues are more likely to carry the virus.

optionRationale.1: Mature leaf cells carry the virus in infected plants.
optionRationale.2: Root hairs are differentiated cells and are not the virus-free tissue used.
optionRationale.4: Woody stem tissue is differentiated and not suitable for this purpose.

questions.objective: Choose the explant for virus-free plants

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Cattle insulin is not used now for most diabetic patients.
Reason (R): Insulin from animal sources may cause allergy or other immune reaction because it is not identical to human insulin.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Earlier insulin was extracted from cattle and pigs. Because it is not exactly the same as human insulin, it could cause allergic reactions. Recombinant human insulin (Humulin) is identical to the human hormone, so it avoids these reactions. R correctly explains A.

optionRationale.2: R is the direct reason for A, so option 2 is not suitable.
optionRationale.3: A is true, because recombinant insulin has largely replaced animal insulin.
optionRationale.4: R is true, because animal insulin differs from human insulin.

questions.objective: Link animal-derived insulin to immune reaction

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about RNA interference.
A. It is a method of cellular defence in eukaryotes.
B. A double-stranded RNA binds to the complementary mRNA and prevents its translation.
C. It was used to protect tobacco plants from the nematode Meloidogyne incognita.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: All three statements are correct. RNAi is a cellular defence of eukaryotes, the complementary dsRNA silences the mRNA by preventing translation, and the method was used to make tobacco resistant to the root-infecting nematode Meloidogyne incognita.

optionRationale.1: C is also correct, so A and B only is incomplete.
optionRationale.2: A is also correct, so B and C only is incomplete.
optionRationale.3: B is also correct, so A and C only is incomplete.

questions.stem: Match the application in List-I with the example in List-II.
questions.explanation: Somatic hybridisation produced the pomato (II). Enzyme deficiency treated by gene therapy refers to ADA deficiency (I). Pest-resistant GM crop is Bt cotton (IV). Cow engineered for human protein is Rosie (III). So A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

optionRationale.2: This option pairs somatic hybridisation with ADA deficiency.
optionRationale.3: This option pairs somatic hybridisation with Rosie.
optionRationale.4: This option pairs somatic hybridisation with Bt cotton.

questions.stem: A PCR run starts with 1 copy of a target DNA segment and every cycle doubles the number of copies. The number of copies after 10 cycles is
questions.explanation: Copies double in each cycle, so after n cycles there are 2^n copies. For n = 10 this is 2^10 = 1024. The number 512 is 2^9 and would be the value after nine cycles, and 2048 would be after eleven.

optionRationale.1: 100 would come from 10 x 10, which is not how doubling works.
optionRationale.2: 512 is the number of copies after only nine cycles.
optionRationale.4: 2048 is the number of copies after eleven cycles.

questions.stem: Gene therapy for ADA deficiency using genetically engineered lymphocytes is not a permanent cure because
options: the retroviral vector destroys the ADA gene
the lymphocytes are not immortal and have to be given repeatedly
ADA enzyme cannot be made by lymphocytes
the gene is deleted again in each generation
questions.explanation: The lymphocytes carrying the functional ADA cDNA are cells of limited life span, so the patient needs periodic infusions. A permanent cure would need the gene to be introduced into early embryonic cells so that it is passed on to all descendants.

optionRationale.1: The vector carries the functional gene and does not destroy it.
optionRationale.3: Lymphocytes do make the enzyme after the cDNA is introduced.
optionRationale.4: The gene is not deleted in each generation; the cells simply die.

questions.objective: Explain why lymphocyte gene therapy is temporary

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Bt toxin kills the insect that eats Bt cotton but does not harm the bacterium that makes it.
Reason (R): The Cry protein is made as an inactive protoxin and is activated by the alkaline pH of the insect midgut.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The protoxin form is harmless to the bacterium. In the alkaline gut of the insect, the crystals dissolve and the activated toxin makes pores in the midgut epithelial cells, which then burst. Thus R explains why A is true.

optionRationale.2: R is the exact explanation of A, so it is more than a mere true statement.
optionRationale.3: A is true because the bacterium is unaffected by its own toxin.
optionRationale.4: R is true because the protoxin is activated by alkaline pH.

questions.objective: Explain selective action of Bt toxin

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.
A. Mature insulin has two chains, A and B, joined by disulphide bridges.
B. The C peptide is present in mature human insulin.
C. Eli Lilly produced chains A and B in separate bacteria for later joining.
D. Mature human insulin has 51 amino acids.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A, C and D are correct. Mature insulin has chain A of 21 and chain B of 30 amino acids (51 in all), joined by disulphide bridges. The two chains were produced separately from DNA sequences and then combined. B is wrong because the C peptide is removed during maturation.

optionRationale.1: B is false: the C peptide is absent from mature insulin.
optionRationale.3: B is false, so any option listing it is wrong.
optionRationale.4: B is false, and this option omits the correct statement D.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on insulin structure and production

questions.stem: In a molecular diagnosis, a radioactive single-stranded DNA probe is used to test cell clones. One clone does not give a signal on the photographic film. The most likely reason is that the clone
options: has a mutated gene that is not complementary to the probe
has too much DNA for the probe
questions.explanation: A probe hybridises only with its complementary sequence. If a clone carries a mutated gene, the mutated sequence is not complementary to the probe, so there is no hybridisation and no signal on the film after autoradiography. This is how mutations are detected.

optionRationale.1: A clone without DNA would not have grown as a clone.
optionRationale.3: More DNA would not prevent hybridisation of a complementary sequence.
optionRationale.4: HIV infection is detected by PCR or ELISA, not by this missing signal.

questions.stem: A company in a developed country patents a trait of a medicinal plant that has been used for centuries by a rural community in a developing country, without informing or paying the community. This situation is best described as
questions.explanation: Biopiracy means use of bio-resources or traditional knowledge by companies or organisations without proper authorisation from the country and people concerned, and without compensatory payment. The example matches this definition exactly.

optionRationale.1: Gene therapy is a medical treatment for genetic disorders.
optionRationale.2: Micropropagation is tissue culture for plant multiplication.
optionRationale.3: RNA interference is a gene silencing mechanism.

questions.stem: A transgenic cow produces milk that has human alpha-lactalbumin at 2.4 grams per litre. How many litres of milk would be required to collect 18 grams of this protein?
questions.explanation: Volume = total mass divided by concentration = 18 g divided by 2.4 g per litre = 7.5 litres. The value 43.2 comes from multiplying 18 by 2.4, which is the wrong operation.

optionRationale.1: 10 litres would give 24 grams, more than needed.
optionRationale.4: 43.2 is the result of multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.objective: Compute volume from concentration of a transgenic product
